scenarios.title: Stuck in the editor
scenarios.situation: You SSH into a server, run 'visudo' to fix sudo access, and land in an unfamiliar full-screen editor. Typing does odd things and you can't figure out how to save or quit.
scenarios.prompt: You're in vim. What is the minimal key sequence to save and exit, and how do you avoid the trap next time?
choices: Press Esc, then type :wq and Enter — and set EDITOR=nano if you prefer nano
Press Ctrl+S to save, then Ctrl+Q to quit, like a GUI editor
Type exit and press Enter — vim understands shell commands directly
Close the terminal — vim auto-saves on disconnect
scenarios.why: Vim is modal: Esc returns to normal mode, and :wq writes and quits. Ctrl+S in a terminal freezes output (XOFF) — the opposite of saving. Setting EDITOR (or VISUAL) to your preferred editor changes what visudo and similar tools open. Never close the terminal on visudo: a half-written sudoers file can lock out sudo.
scenarios.hint: What does the Esc key do in a modal editor?

scenarios.title: The commented-out setting
scenarios.situation: A config file has '#PasswordAuthentication yes' and you must ensure the active line reads 'PasswordAuthentication no'. There are 200 similar files across hosts and you want a one-liner.
scenarios.prompt: Which sed command does this correctly?
choices: sed -i 's/^#\?PasswordAuthentication.*/PasswordAuthentication no/' sshd_config
sed 's/PasswordAuthentication/no/' sshd_config > sshd_config
sed -i 'd/PasswordAuthentication/' sshd_config
sed -i 's/yes/no/' sshd_config
scenarios.why: The pattern anchors to line start, optionally matches the '#', then replaces the whole PasswordAuthentication line regardless of its current value. -i edits in place. Redirecting sed output back into the same file truncates it (the shell empties the file before sed reads it). The bare 's/yes/no/' would also mangle unrelated 'yes' values like PermitRootLogin.
scenarios.hint: Which lines should match — commented, uncommented, or both?

scenarios.title: The doubled directory
scenarios.situation: You run 'rsync -av /srv/www/ /backup/www/' nightly. After a manual run of 'rsync -av /srv/www /backup/www/' you find /backup/www/www/ with a full duplicate tree.
scenarios.prompt: What does the trailing slash on the source change, and how do you fix the layout?
choices: A trailing slash copies the directory's contents; without it, rsync copies the directory itself — rerun with the slash and remove the nested copy
The trailing slash enables compression; rerun without -z to fix it
The trailing slash means 'dry run'; the duplicate came from something else
Rsync always duplicates one level — this is expected behavior
scenarios.why: This is rsync's most famous gotcha: 'src/' transfers the contents of src into dest, while 'src' transfers the directory src itself into dest (creating dest/src). The fix is to rerun with the trailing slash for future syncs and delete the accidental nested /backup/www/www tree.
scenarios.hint: Compare what 'cp -r src/ dest' vs 'cp -r src dest' would do.

scenarios.title: Which package owns this file?
scenarios.situation: A monitoring script fails because /usr/bin/jq is missing on a fresh RHEL install. You need the package name to install it, but you're not sure which package provides jq.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right dnf query?
choices: dnf provides /usr/bin/jq — then dnf install the owning package
dnf search jq — only searches package names, which is enough
rpm -qa | grep jq — lists only installed packages, so it can't help
dnf install /usr/bin/jq — dnf cannot install by file path
scenarios.why: 'dnf provides <path>' (or '*/jq') maps a file path to the package that ships it, querying repository metadata — not just installed packages. 'dnf install <filepath>' actually also works via provides, but 'provides' is the explicit discovery step. rpm -qa only sees what's already installed.
scenarios.hint: Which tool can search the repositories, not just the local RPM database?

scenarios.title: The web server died at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: httpd stopped overnight. You need its logs from the failure window, the most recent entries first isn't helpful — you want to follow new entries live while you restart it.
scenarios.prompt: Which journalctl invocation fits?
choices: journalctl -u httpd --since '02:00' -f — unit logs since 2 AM, following live
journalctl /var/log/httpd/error_log — journalctl reads flat files directly
dmesg | grep httpd — kernel ring buffer holds service logs
journalctl -u httpd > /dev/null — discarding output refreshes the log
scenarios.why: -u filters by systemd unit, --since bounds the window, and -f follows new entries like tail -f. journalctl queries the systemd journal, not flat files (that's what -u is for). dmesg shows kernel messages only, and redirecting to /dev/null just throws output away.
scenarios.hint: Which flags select a service, a time window, and live-follow?

scenarios.title: Works until reboot
scenarios.situation: You run 'systemctl start nginx' and the site works — until the next reboot, when it's down again. The service file exists in /usr/lib/systemd/system.
scenarios.prompt: What was missed, and what's the one command that does both?
choices: The service was started but not enabled — 'systemctl enable --now nginx' does both
The service needs 'systemctl load nginx' before it survives reboot
Nginx can't start at boot without a cron @reboot entry
The unit file must be copied to /etc/systemd/system to persist
scenarios.why: start affects the current runtime only; enable creates the symlink (typically into multi-user.target.wants) that pulls the service in at boot. 'enable --now' combines both in one command. Unit files in /usr/lib/systemd/system are the packaged defaults — enabling never requires copying them.
scenarios.hint: Which systemctl verb controls boot-time behavior vs right-now behavior?

scenarios.title: Core Tools: Design Decision
scenarios.situation: You need to make an architecture/design decision for Core Tools in a Rhcsa environment. Multiple approaches are viable, but each has tradeoffs.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach best balances the competing concerns for this Core Tools scenario?
choices: Analyze the requirements, evaluate each option against constraints (performance, cost, complexity, maintainability), select the approach with the best tradeoff profile, and document the decision rationale including rejected alternatives.
Choose the most familiar approach — comfort matters more than fit.
Choose the newest technology — latest is always best.
Delay the decision — more analysis is always better.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Architecture decisions require structured evaluation: (1) Clarify requirements and constraints, (2) Enumerate viable options, (3) Score each against weighted criteria, (4) Select the best tradeoff, (5) Document why others were rejected. This prevents both analysis paralysis and reckless choices in Core Tools design.
scenarios.hint: Think about how senior engineers make decisions — it's not gut feel, it's structured evaluation.
evidence: Review Core Tools requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: Core Tools: Expert Scenario
scenarios.situation: An advanced Core Tools challenge in a Rhcsa environment requires expert-level judgment. The situation involves multiple interacting factors.
scenarios.prompt: What is the expert-level approach to this Core Tools challenge?
choices: Systematically analyze all factors, prioritize by impact and urgency, implement the solution with verification at each step, and document the approach for the team.
Apply the most common solution immediately without analysis.
Defer to someone else — this is too complex.
Try random approaches until something works.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Expert Core Tools work in Rhcsa requires: systematic analysis (understand all factors), prioritization (impact × urgency), verified implementation (check each step), and documentation (team learning). This disciplined approach distinguishes senior practitioners.
scenarios.hint: What separates expert practice from guessing?

scenarios.title: Onboarding the web developer
scenarios.situation: A new developer needs an account: home directory, bash shell, membership in the 'webdev' group, and a comment with her full name.
scenarios.prompt: Which useradd invocation does all of this?
choices: useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G webdev -c 'Ana Torres' ana
useradd ana (then hand-edit /etc/passwd for the rest)
adduser --no-home --shell /bin/sh ana
useradd -G webdev ana (groups imply home and shell)
scenarios.why: -m creates the home directory (skel files included), -s sets the login shell, -G adds supplementary groups, -c sets the GECOS/comment field. Hand-editing /etc/passwd bypasses validation — use the tools. Verify with 'id ana'.
scenarios.hint: Which flags control home, shell, groups, and comment separately?

scenarios.title: The vanishing groups
scenarios.situation: You run 'usermod -G docker ana' to give Ana docker access. She reports she can use docker now — but lost access to the webdev group she had before.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what's the fix?
choices: -G without -a REPLACES the supplementary group list — use 'usermod -aG docker ana' to append
Users can only be in one group — remove webdev permanently
usermod requires a reboot to take effect — wait and recheck
Group changes need 'newgrp' run as root first
scenarios.why: usermod -G sets the complete supplementary group list, wiping previous memberships — the classic footgun. -aG appends instead. Always verify with 'id ana' or 'groups ana' after changes. (Also note: group membership changes apply at next login.)
scenarios.hint: Does -G add to the list, or replace the list?

scenarios.title: The contractor account
scenarios.situation: A contractor's account must stop working on 2027-01-15, and her password must expire every 60 days with a 7-day warning.
scenarios.prompt: Which commands implement this?
choices: chage -E 2027-01-15 contractor && chage -M 60 -W 7 contractor
passwd -e contractor (sets both account and password expiry)
usermod -L contractor (locks until the date passes)
Edit /etc/shadow by hand — chage can't set dates
scenarios.why: chage manages aging: -E sets the account expiry date (login disabled after), -M max password lifetime in days, -W warning days before expiry. passwd -e only forces password change at next login; usermod -L locks the account immediately. 'chage -l user' lists the current policy.
scenarios.hint: Which tool manages both account expiry dates and password aging?

scenarios.title: One extra reader, no new group
scenarios.situation: Directory /srv/project is owned by group 'eng' (rwx). An auditor needs read access to one file — but must NOT be added to eng, and permissions on the file must stay 640.
scenarios.prompt: What mechanism grants this exception?
choices: A POSIX ACL: 'setfacl -m u:auditor:r /srv/project/report.txt' — verify with getfacl
chmod 644 — simplest and good enough
chown auditor — ownership transfer is the only way
Add auditor to eng temporarily, then remove her
scenarios.why: ACLs (setfacl/getfacl) attach per-user/per-group permission entries beyond the owner/group/other triple — the '+' in ls -l flags their presence. chmod 644 would expose the file to everyone; chown changes ownership semantics. Note the ACL mask: the entry's effective permission is ANDed with the mask.
scenarios.hint: What extends the classic three permission triples with named-user entries?

scenarios.title: Let deploy restart nginx
scenarios.situation: The 'deploy' user must run only 'systemctl restart nginx' as root, without a password. Directly editing /etc/sudoers is discouraged.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe approach?
choices: Create /etc/sudoers.d/deploy with 'deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx' and validate with 'visudo -c'
Add 'deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to /etc/sudoers directly
Set the setuid bit on systemctl so deploy can run it
Give deploy the root password — simplest
scenarios.why: /etc/sudoers.d/ drop-in files keep custom rules separate from the packaged sudoers file (which updates won't clobber). The rule grants one exact command as root with no password. 'visudo -c' syntax-checks before the change goes live — a sudoers syntax error can lock out all sudo access, which is why direct editing without visudo is dangerous.
scenarios.hint: Where do you put a sudo rule so a package update won't overwrite it?

scenarios.title: Root's PATH mystery
scenarios.situation: You 'su' to root and run a sbin tool — 'command not found'. Your colleague does 'su -', runs the same tool, and it works.
scenarios.prompt: What differs between su and su -?
choices: 'su -' starts a login shell with root's full environment (including /usr/sbin in PATH); plain 'su' keeps your environment
'su' is an alias for sudo — it doesn't actually change users
The tool only exists in the colleague's home directory
su - enables SELinux; su doesn't
scenarios.why: 'su -' (or 'su -l') simulates a full login: root's profile scripts run, giving root's PATH (with /usr/sbin, /sbin), HOME, and working directory. Plain 'su' keeps your environment — convenient but a classic source of 'command not found' for admin tools and a subtle security consideration.
scenarios.hint: Whose PATH do you have after each variant?

scenarios.title: Users & Groups: Production Incident
scenarios.situation: A production Users & Groups system is experiencing degraded performance. Users are affected. You need to diagnose and resolve quickly without making things worse.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response sequence for this Users & Groups degradation?
choices: Assess impact and declare incident severity, check recent changes (deployments, config changes), review key metrics to isolate the layer, implement the least-risky mitigation first, verify recovery, then conduct a blameless post-mortem.
Immediately restart all Users & Groups components — fastest way to resolve.
Roll back the last deployment without investigation — it's always the deployment.
Wait and monitor — it might resolve itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Incident response follows: (1) Assess impact (how bad? who's affected?), (2) Check recent changes (what changed?), (3) Isolate via metrics (which layer?), (4) Mitigate with least risk (don't make it worse), (5) Verify recovery, (6) Post-mortem (prevent recurrence). Skipping steps in Users & Groups incidents causes extended outages.
scenarios.hint: Remember the incident response phases from the lessons. What's the order?
evidence: Review Users & Groups requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: The disk that moved
scenarios.situation: After adding a new disk, /dev/sdb became /dev/sdc and the data volume failed to mount at boot. The fstab entry used /dev/sdb1.
scenarios.prompt: What is the robust fix?
choices: Mount by UUID (or LABEL) instead of device name — UUIDs are stable across rescans; get it from 'blkid'
Rename the device back with mv /dev/sdc1 /dev/sdb1
Use /dev/disk/by-path — it's shorter
Remove the fstab entry and mount manually after each boot
scenarios.why: Kernel device names (sda, sdb) are assigned in discovery order and can shift when hardware changes. UUIDs and LABELs are written on the filesystem and never change — 'UUID=xxx /data xfs defaults 0 2' survives rescans. Always run 'mount -a' to validate fstab before rebooting.
scenarios.hint: What identifies the filesystem itself rather than its plug-in order?

scenarios.title: /var is full — extend it live
scenarios.situation: /var on logical volume vg0/lv_var (xfs) hit 100%. The volume group has 20G free. The filesystem must stay online.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sequence?
choices: lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vg0/lv_var — extends the LV and grows xfs online in one step
umount /var, lvextend, mkfs.xfs, mount — the safe full cycle
lvextend then xfs_shrink — XFS grows automatically
Add a second mount on top of /var — overlay doubles the space
scenarios.why: lvextend grows the block device; '-r/--resizefs' then grows the filesystem appropriately (xfs_growfs for XFS, resize2fs for ext4) — online, no unmount. XFS can only grow, never shrink; ext4 can do both (shrinking requires unmount + e2fsck). 'vgs'/'lvs' confirm free space first.
scenarios.hint: Which single flag makes lvextend handle the filesystem too?

scenarios.title: New disk for the database
scenarios.situation: A fresh /dev/sdc (100G) must become a 60G logical volume 'lv_db' in a new volume group 'vg_db', formatted xfs and mounted at /db.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct order of operations?
choices: pvcreate /dev/sdc → vgcreate vg_db /dev/sdc → lvcreate -n lv_db -L 60G vg_db → mkfs.xfs → mount + fstab entry
mkfs.xfs /dev/sdc → pvcreate → mount — format first
vgcreate then pvcreate — groups come before physical volumes
lvcreate directly on /dev/sdc — LVM auto-creates PV/VG
scenarios.why: LVM layers bottom-up: PV (physical volume on the disk/partition) → VG (pool) → LV (carved from the pool) → filesystem → mount. pvcreate labels the device, vgcreate pools it, lvcreate carves the LV, mkfs creates the filesystem, then mount/fstab. Skipping layers breaks the abstraction.
scenarios.hint: Which layer must exist before you can carve a logical volume from it?

scenarios.title: Can we shrink /var?
scenarios.situation: /var (xfs, 50G, 10G used) is overprovisioned. The team wants to shrink it to 20G and give the space to /home (also xfs).
scenarios.prompt: What do you tell them?
choices: XFS cannot be shrunk, period — back up /var, recreate the LV smaller, restore; or take space from elsewhere
Use lvreduce -r — it handles XFS shrinking automatically
xfs_growfs with a negative size shrinks it
Shrink while mounted — XFS supports online shrink
scenarios.why: XFS is grow-only by design — there is no shrink support (xfs_growfs only grows). To reclaim space: back up the data, recreate the filesystem smaller, restore. This is a planning lesson: size XFS volumes conservatively, or use ext4/stratis where shrinkability matters. lvreduce on an XFS LV corrupts data.
scenarios.hint: What does xfs_growfs do — and what tool would do the opposite?

scenarios.title: Trying Stratis for the file share
scenarios.situation: You want pooled storage with thin provisioning and snapshots for /srv/share, without hand-managing LVM. The disk is /dev/sdd.
scenarios.prompt: What is the Stratis workflow?
choices: stratis pool create pool1 /dev/sdd → stratis filesystem create pool1 share → mount the /dev/stratis/pool1/share device; snapshots via 'stratis filesystem snapshot'
stratis is a filesystem type — mkfs.stratis /dev/sdd
Stratis pools are created with vgcreate — it's just LVM
Mount /dev/sdd directly — Stratis works without setup
scenarios.why: Stratis is a storage manager (daemon + CLI) simplifying pool/filesystem/snapshot management atop device-mapper+XFS: create a pool from block devices, create thin filesystems in it, mount via /dev/stratis/<pool>/<fs>. Snapshots are first-class ('filesystem snapshot'). Ensure stratisd is running and enabled.
scenarios.hint: What are Stratis's three layers — pool, filesystem, and what operation for point-in-time copies?

scenarios.title: Adding emergency swap
scenarios.situation: A VM with no swap partition is under memory pressure. You have disk space but can't repartition right now.
scenarios.prompt: How do you add a 2G swap file correctly?
choices: fallocate -l 2G /swapfile; chmod 600 /swapfile; mkswap /swapfile; swapon /swapfile; add fstab entry
dd a file and swapon it — permissions don't matter for swap
mkswap on a directory — swap works on any path
Swap files aren't supported on Linux — only partitions
scenarios.why: Swap files work like swap partitions: allocate (fallocate/dd), chmod 600 (a world-readable swap file leaks memory contents), mkswap to format, swapon to activate, fstab entry ('/swapfile swap swap defaults 0 0') for persistence. 'swapon -s'/'free' verifies. Prefer a partition for hibernation, but files are fine for pressure relief.
scenarios.hint: Why would a swap file need restrictive permissions?

scenarios.title: Storage (LVM/Stratis): Code Review Finding
scenarios.situation: During code review, you notice a Storage (LVM/Stratis) implementation that works but has potential issues. The author is a junior developer who is eager to merge.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle this Storage (LVM/Stratis) code review as a senior team member?
choices: Provide specific, actionable feedback: explain the issue, why it matters, suggest a concrete fix, and offer to pair on the solution. Approve the approach but request changes on the implementation.
Approve immediately — it works, and you don't want to discourage the junior.
Reject outright with 'this is wrong' — they'll figure it out.
Rewrite the code yourself — faster than explaining.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Effective code review for Storage (LVM/Stratis): (1) Be specific about the issue (not 'this is bad'), (2) Explain the impact (why it matters), (3) Suggest a fix (don't just criticize), (4) Offer help (mentorship). This builds both better Storage (LVM/Stratis) code and better engineers.
scenarios.hint: Think about the goal of code review — it's not just gatekeeping, it's team growth.

scenarios.title: Replacing cron with a timer
scenarios.situation: A cron job runs /usr/local/bin/backup.sh daily at 2 AM, but cron emails failures into a void and you want journal-integrated logging plus 'run if the machine was off at 2 AM'.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two unit files, and what does the timer add?
choices: backup.service (the job) + backup.timer (OnCalendar=daily, Persistent=true) — timers give journal logging, dependencies, and Persistent catches up missed runs
A .timer alone — it embeds the command
cron can't be replaced — timers are only for boot tasks
One .service with Cron= enabled — systemd reads crontabs
scenarios.why: systemd timers split schedule (.timer: OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00, Persistent=true, Unit=) from work (.service: ExecStart=). Advantages over cron: logs in the journal (journalctl -u backup), dependency ordering, randomized delays (RandomizedDelaySec), and Persistent=true runs the job once if the window was missed (laptops/VMs that were off). 'systemctl list-timers' shows the schedule.
scenarios.hint: Which unit holds the schedule, and which holds the command?

scenarios.title: Server boots to a GUI
scenarios.situation: A RHEL server boots into the graphical login, wasting RAM on a headless box. You want text-mode multi-user boot.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and how do targets relate to runlevels?
choices: systemctl set-default multi-user.target — targets are systemd's runlevels; multi-user ≈ runlevel 3, graphical ≈ 5
Delete the GUI packages — the only way
systemctl disable gdm — that changes the default target
Edit /etc/inittab — still the authoritative file
scenarios.why: Targets group units like SysV runlevels did: rescue (≈1), multi-user (≈3), graphical (≈5). set-default symlinks default.target. 'systemctl isolate multi-user.target' switches now without reboot. Disabling gdm alone doesn't change the default target — set-default is the correct persistent change.
scenarios.hint: Which command changes the boot-time default target persistently?

scenarios.title: Locked out of root
scenarios.situation: The root password is lost on a RHEL VM (console access available). You need to reset it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rd.break procedure?
choices: Interrupt GRUB, append rd.break to the linux line, boot; mount -o remount,rw /sysroot; chroot /sysroot; passwd; touch /.autorelabel; exit twice
Boot normally and run passwd — it doesn't need the old password
Reinstall — lost root passwords are unrecoverable
rd.break only works on Ubuntu
scenarios.why: rd.break drops to a shell in the initramfs before the real root mounts: remount /sysroot read-write, chroot into it, passwd resets root, and /.autorelabel is critical — without it, SELinux denies login after the password file change. Then exit the chroot and exit again to continue boot. This is why console/bootloader access must be physically secured.
scenarios.hint: Why is the /.autorelabel step essential on an SELinux system?

scenarios.title: Reading the crontab
scenarios.situation: You inherit '*/15 9-17 * * 1-5 /opt/report.sh' in a crontab and need to explain when it runs.
scenarios.prompt: Decode the schedule.
choices: Every 15 minutes, between 09:00–17:59, Monday–Friday — fields are minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week
Every 15 seconds during business hours
At 9:15 AM and 5:15 PM on weekdays
Every 15 minutes all day, every day
scenarios.why: Crontab fields: minute(0-59) hour(0-23) dom(1-31) month(1-12) dow(0-7). */15 = every 15 min, 9-17 = hours 9–17, * = any dom/month, 1-5 = Mon–Fri. User crontabs (crontab -e) run as that user; /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d add a user field. Remember cron's minimal PATH and that output is mailed (or configure logging).
scenarios.hint: How many time fields are there, and what order?

scenarios.title: The service that keeps coming back
scenarios.situation: You disabled cups, but a dependency keeps starting it. 'systemctl disable' isn't enough.
scenarios.prompt: What stronger measure exists, and when is it appropriate?
choices: systemctl mask cups — symlinks the unit to /dev/null so it can't be started even manually; use for services that must never run
systemctl stop — stronger than disable
Delete the unit file — the clean approach
mask is the same as disable — the dependency is a bug
scenarios.why: disable removes boot-time symlinks but the unit can still be started manually or pulled in as a dependency. mask links it to /dev/null, making any start attempt fail. Use masking for services that must never run (security hardening); unmask to restore. Deleting unit files breaks package updates — never do that.
scenarios.hint: What is stronger than 'don't start at boot'?

scenarios.title: Logs gone after reboot
scenarios.situation: After a crash-reboot, 'journalctl --since "1 hour ago"' shows nothing from before the reboot. The team needs persistent journals for post-crash forensics.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the journal survive reboots?
choices: Create /var/log/journal (systemd-journald then persists to disk) and/or set Storage=persistent in journald.conf
Journals are always persistent — the crash corrupted them
Install rsyslog — journald can't persist
journalctl --persist — enables it per query
scenarios.why: By default journald keeps logs in /run (tmpfs) — lost on reboot. Creating /var/log/journal flips it to persistent disk storage (or Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf). Also consider SystemMaxUse/MaxRetentionSec to bound disk usage, and ForwardToSyslog if you also run rsyslog. Verify with 'journalctl --list-boots'.
scenarios.hint: Where does the journal live by default — disk or RAM?

Delay the decision — more analysis is always better.

scenarios.title: Setting a static IP
scenarios.situation: Server db1 needs static IP 10.0.5.20/24, gateway 10.0.5.1, DNS 10.0.5.2 on connection 'eth0'. No GUI available.
scenarios.prompt: What is the nmcli sequence?
choices: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 10.0.5.20/24 ipv4.gateway 10.0.5.1 ipv4.dns 10.0.5.2 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0
ifconfig eth0 10.0.5.20 — persistent and sufficient
Edit /etc/resolv.conf — that sets the IP address
nmcli con mod eth0 ip 10.0.5.20 — the key is 'ip'
scenarios.why: nmcli con mod sets properties on the connection profile: ipv4.addresses (CIDR), ipv4.gateway, ipv4.dns, ipv4.method manual (vs auto/DHCP). Changes apply on 'nmcli con up'. ifconfig is deprecated (use 'ip addr') and non-persistent. Verify with 'ip addr show' and 'nmcli con show eth0'.
scenarios.hint: Which subcommand modifies a connection profile, and which activates it?

scenarios.title: Opening the web port
scenarios.situation: nginx serves locally (curl localhost works) but remote clients time out. The server uses firewalld, zone 'public'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you open HTTP persistently?
choices: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http && firewall-cmd --reload (or --add-port=80/tcp)
firewall-cmd --add-service=http — permanent by default
iptables -A INPUT -j ACCEPT — firewalld is just a frontend, edit iptables directly
systemctl stop firewalld — simplest fix
scenarios.why: firewalld runtime changes vanish on reload unless --permanent (then --reload applies them). --add-service=http opens 80/tcp via the service definition; --add-port=8080/tcp for custom ports. Verify with --list-all --zone=public. Disabling the firewall 'fixes' connectivity by removing security — never the answer.
scenarios.hint: What makes a firewall-cmd change survive a reload?

scenarios.title: 403 after moving the web root
scenarios.situation: You move the website from /var/www to /srv/www, update nginx, and get 403 Forbidden. Permissions are 755, nginx runs as nginx user, and the error log says 'Permission denied'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the likely cause and the persistent fix?
choices: SELinux file context — /srv/www lacks httpd_sys_content_t; fix persistently with 'semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/www(/.*)?" && restorecon -Rv /srv/www'
chmod 777 /srv/www — SELinux doesn't affect nginx
chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t — persistent across relabels
Disable SELinux — the standard fix for 403s
scenarios.why: 'Permission denied' with correct Unix permissions screams SELinux (check /var/log/audit/audit.log or 'ausearch -m avc'). chcon changes context temporarily — a filesystem relabel or restorecon reverts it. semanage fcontext writes the policy mapping so the context persists. Never disable SELinux to fix a context problem.
scenarios.hint: Which tool makes a context change survive a relabel?

scenarios.title: nginx can't reach the app server
scenarios.situation: nginx (as reverse proxy) gets 'Permission denied' connecting to the app on 127.0.0.1:3000. Curl from the shell works. AVC denials mention httpd and name_connect.
scenarios.prompt: What is the targeted fix?
choices: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on — allows httpd scripts/modules to make network connections, persistently
setenforce 0 — quick and permanent
Allow all: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on is the same thing
Open port 3000 in firewalld — SELinux follows firewall rules
scenarios.why: SELinux booleans toggle policy capabilities: httpd_can_network_connect lets the web server initiate outbound connections (reverse proxying). -P makes it persistent (without -P it's runtime-only). The _db variant is narrower (database ports only). 'getsebool -a | grep httpd' lists them. setenforce 0 is runtime-only AND disables protection — not a fix.
scenarios.hint: Which boolean governs httpd-initiated network connections?

scenarios.title: Renaming the server
scenarios.situation: Server 'localhost' needs to become 'web1.example.com' persistently, and other hosts should resolve it.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two steps?
choices: hostnamectl set-hostname web1.example.com (persistent) + add '10.0.5.10 web1.example.com web1' to /etc/hosts (or DNS)
hostname web1 — persistent across reboots
Edit /etc/hostname by hand — hostnamectl is deprecated
/etc/hosts alone renames the machine
scenarios.why: hostnamectl set-hostname writes /etc/hostname persistently (transient 'hostname' doesn't survive reboot). Name resolution is separate: /etc/hosts for small setups or real DNS. Check with 'hostnamectl' and 'getent hosts web1.example.com'.
scenarios.hint: Which command persists the hostname, and where does resolution come from?

scenarios.title: Hardening SSH
scenarios.situation: Audit flags: root login allowed, password auth on, default port 22 getting brute-forced. You need key-only auth for a deploy user, no root login.
scenarios.prompt: What sshd_config changes, and how do you apply them safely?
choices: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no (with keys deployed first!), then 'sshd -t && systemctl reload sshd' — test config before reloading
Port 2222 alone — obscurity is sufficient security
Delete /etc/ssh/sshd_config — defaults are secure
systemctl restart sshd without testing — reload is for cowards
scenarios.why: Harden in /etc/ssh/sshd_config: PermitRootLogin no (or prohibit-password), PasswordAuthentication no ONLY after verifying key auth works (lock yourself out otherwise!), consider AllowUsers. 'sshd -t' validates syntax; 'systemctl reload sshd' applies without dropping existing sessions (restart would too, but reload is gentler). Keep one spare session open while testing.
scenarios.hint: What must you verify BEFORE disabling password authentication?

scenarios.title: First container on RHEL
scenarios.situation: You need nginx running detached, port 8080→80, with persistent data in a named volume, on RHEL where Docker isn't the default.
scenarios.prompt: What is the podman command, and how does podman differ from Docker here?
choices: podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -v webdata:/usr/share/nginx/html nginx — podman is daemonless and CLI-compatible with Docker
podman needs a daemon started first — systemctl start docker
Docker commands don't work with podman — learn a new CLI
Containers can't run unprivileged — use sudo for everything
scenarios.why: Podman mirrors the Docker CLI (alias docker=podman is common) but runs daemonless — containers are child processes, and rootless Podman runs entirely as your user. -d detached, -p publish, -v volume. 'podman images/containers/ps' all work. On RHEL, podman + buildah + skopeo replace the Docker engine.
scenarios.hint: What daemon does podman need running?

scenarios.title: Container must survive reboot
scenarios.situation: Your podman container runs fine, but after reboot it's gone (well — exited). You need it managed like a service.
scenarios.prompt: How do you run a rootless container under systemd?
choices: podman generate systemd --new --name web > ~/.config/systemd/user/container-web.service, then systemctl --user enable --now (with lingering enabled)
Add it to /etc/rc.local — the traditional way
podman run --restart=always — podman has Docker-style restart policies built in
Containers can't auto-start — start them manually
scenarios.why: podman generate systemd creates a unit that runs 'podman start/stop' for the container; --new uses 'podman run' so the container is recreated. As a user unit it needs 'loginctl enable-linger <user>' to run without an active session. Quadlets (.container files) are the newer declarative alternative. (Recent podman does support --restart policies too, but systemd integration is the RHEL-native answer.)
scenarios.hint: Who manages services that must start at boot?

scenarios.title: Permission denied inside the container
scenarios.situation: You mount /srv/data into a podman container. The app gets permission denied, though host permissions look fine. 'ls -Z' shows the files labeled default_t.
scenarios.prompt: What is the SELinux-aware fix?
choices: Append :z (shared) or :Z (private) to the -v mount — podman relabels the content to container_file_t so the container can access it
setenforce 0 — containers and SELinux don't mix
chmod 777 /srv/data — SELinux follows Unix permissions
Run with --privileged — the standard fix
scenarios.why: Container processes run under a confined SELinux domain and can only touch container_file_t labeled content. :z relabels for shared access (multiple containers), :Z for exclusive (private unshared) access. --privileged disables nearly all isolation — a sledgehammer for a labeling problem. Check denials with ausearch -m avc.
scenarios.hint: What label must mounted content carry for the container domain to read it?

scenarios.title: Web-based server check
scenarios.situation: You're away from your SSH keys but have a browser. You need to check service status, storage, and logs on the RHEL server.
scenarios.prompt: What is available natively, and on which port?
choices: Cockpit — the web console on port 9090 (cockpit.socket), covering services, storage, logs, networking, and containers
RHEL has no web console — install third-party software
Port 80 — the web server doubles as admin console
Cockpit is a separate paid product
scenarios.why: Cockpit ships with RHEL: 'systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket' serves https://server:9090 with system login. It manages systemd services, storage (incl. LVM/Stratis views), journals, networking, user accounts, and podman containers — ideal for quick checks and for junior admins. It's included, not an add-on.
scenarios.hint: Which port does the built-in web console listen on?

scenarios.title: Rootless port binding fails
scenarios.situation: Running rootless podman, '-p 80:80' fails with permission denied, but '-p 8080:80' works.
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what are the options?
choices: Unprivileged users can't bind ports < 1024 — use a high port, or set net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=80 via sysctl
Podman can't publish ports at all rootless
Port 80 is always in use — pick another
Rootless containers have no network — expected
scenarios.why: The kernel restricts sub-1024 binds to privileged processes — rootless containers inherit this. Options: publish high ports (8080→80), or lower net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start (e.g., to 80) via sysctl. This is a security feature, not a podman limitation — the same applies to any unprivileged process.
scenarios.hint: Which port numbers are privileged, and who enforces that?

scenarios.title: New server checklist
scenarios.situation: A fresh RHEL server will face the internet. You need the baseline hardening pass.
scenarios.prompt: What are the essential first steps?
choices: Update all packages, enable firewalld with minimal open ports, SSH key-only + no root login, enable SELinux enforcing, enable automatic updates or a patch cadence
Disable the firewall for easier debugging, then harden later
Change the SSH port — that's sufficient hardening
Hardening is optional on cloud VMs — the provider handles it
scenarios.why: Baseline: dnf update (patch known CVEs), firewalld default-deny with only needed services, sshd hardening (keys, no root, no password auth), SELinux enforcing (confinement when something breaks in), and a sustained patch process (dnf-automatic or scheduled). Port changes are obscurity, not security — do them only atop real controls.
scenarios.hint: Which of these actually reduces attack surface vs just hiding it?

concepts: Vim is modal: Esc returns to normal mode, and :wq writes and quits.
sed: redirecting sed output back into the same file truncates it (the shell empties the file before sed reads it).

rsync semantics: this is rsync's most famous gotcha: 'src/' transfers the contents of src into dest, while 'src' transfers the directory src itself into dest (creating dest/src).

lessons.title: Users & Groups — Core concepts
concepts: Account creation: chage manages aging: -E sets the account expiry date (login disabled after), -M max password lifetime in days, -W warning days before expiry. passwd -e only forces password change at next login; usermod -L locks the account immediately.

lessons.title: Storage (LVM/Stratis) — Core concepts
concepts: LVM layers bottom-up: PV (physical volume on the disk/partition) → VG (pool) → LV (carved from the pool) → filesystem → mount. pvcreate labels the device, vgcreate pools it, lvcreate carves the LV, mkfs creates the filesystem, then mount/fstab.

fstab: swap files work like swap partitions: allocate (fallocate/dd), chmod 600 (a world-readable swap file leaks memory contents), mkswap to format, swapon to activate, fstab entry ('/swapfile swap swap defaults 0 0') for persistence.
UUIDs and LABELs are written on the filesystem and never change — 'UUID=xxx /data xfs defaults 0 2' survives rescans.
Lvextend grows the block device; '-r/--resizefs' then grows the filesystem appropriately (xfs_growfs for XFS, resize2fs for ext4) — online, no unmount.
XFS can only grow, never shrink; ext4 can do both (shrinking requires unmount + e2fsck). XFS is grow-only by design — there is no shrink support (xfs_growfs only grows).

example.code: /dev/sdb1  /data  xfs  defaults  0 2
example.walkthrough: Kernel device names (sda, sdb) are assigned in discovery order and can shift when hardware changes. Always run 'mount -a' to validate fstab before rebooting.

pitfalls: Common trap: swap files aren't supported on Linux.
Common trap: stratis pools are created with vgcreate.
Common trap: remove the fstab entry and mount manually after each boot.

lessons.title: RHCSA — Core concepts
concepts: systemd is the init system: 'systemctl start/stop' changes the now, 'systemctl enable/disable' changes what happens at boot, and 'systemctl status' shows both plus recent log lines.
Storage on RHEL is layered — disk, partition or PV, volume group, logical volume, filesystem — and each layer has its own tool (lsblk, pvs/vgs/lvs, mkfs, mount), so diagnose at the right layer.
firewalld manages the host firewall through zones and services; '--permanent' writes config and '--reload' applies it, while runtime-only changes vanish on reload.

SELinux enforces mandatory access control by type: processes run in domains (httpd_t) and files carry types (httpd_sys_content_t); denials are diagnosed with ausearch and fixed with semanage fcontext + restorecon.
Podman runs OCI containers daemonless and rootless by default on RHEL; rootless containers cannot bind privileged ports (<1024) or access host devices without explicit delegation.
User and group management (useradd, usermod, groupadd) is file-based in /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group — understand the files and the tools become obvious.

example.code:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services
example.walkthrough: The first command writes the http service into the permanent configuration of the active zone. '--reload' applies permanent config to the runtime without dropping connections. The last command confirms http is now listed.

pitfalls: Common trap: editing unit files under /usr/lib/systemd/system — they are package-owned and your changes vanish on update; use 'systemctl edit' for drop-ins.
Common trap: using chcon for an SELinux labeling fix — it works until the next relabel; semanage fcontext is the persistent fix.
Common trap: forgetting '--permanent' on firewall-cmd — the rule works until the next reload, then silently disappears.
Common trap: extending a logical volume but forgetting to grow the filesystem (xfs_growfs / resize2fs) — the space stays invisible to df.

lessons.title: RHCSA Spine — Core concepts
concepts: Boot is a chain — firmware, GRUB2, kernel, systemd: each stage's success is visible on the console, so localize failures by finding the last stage that completed.
systemd targets (rescue, multi-user, graphical) are synchronization points; 'systemd.unit=' on the kernel command line boots into any of them for recovery.
LVM separates physical disks (PVs) from usable space (VGs) from filesystems (LVs): extend at each layer in order, and use snapshots for instant pre-change rollback points.
XFS (RHEL default) grows online but never shrinks — 'lvextend -r' handles LV plus filesystem in one step; ext4 uses resize2fs and can do both.
Linux routing is longest-match: connected subnet routes beat defaults, and a host should have exactly one default gateway — a second default is a classic post-reboot breakage.
Troubleshoot in isolation order: process listening (ss), service state and logs (systemctl, journalctl), host firewall (firewall-cmd), then the network — prove each layer before blaming the next.

example.code:
sudo lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vg_sys/lv_var
df -h /var
sudo lvs
example.walkthrough: Extends the logical volume by 10 GB and, via -r, grows the filesystem online in the same command. df confirms the new space is visible; lvs shows the LV's new size. No unmount, no downtime.

pitfalls: Common trap: growing the LV but not the filesystem — df won't show new space until xfs_growfs/resize2fs runs; '-r' prevents this.
Common trap: shrinking XFS — impossible; plan LV sizes accordingly or use ext4 where shrink is needed.
Common trap: two default gateways after adding a NIC — remove the spurious one; connected routes already cover the local subnet.
Common trap: editing fstab with device names (/dev/sdb1) — names shift; use UUIDs from blkid.

lessons.title: How to Use This Red Hat Certified System Administrator Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: course overview, study strategy, key terminology) → Lessons (the deep-dives, in domain order) → Drills (practice scenarios, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on exercises) → Mock Assessment (timed simulation). Each layer assumes the one before. Skipping straight to the mock burns your one realistic practice run.

What 'Linux system administrator' means in practice: this bootcamp prepares you for the real-world responsibilities of a Linux system administrator, not just exam questions. Every lesson connects theory to the decisions you'll make on the job — what to check first, what to try next, how to explain your reasoning.

The EX200 Red Hat Certified System Administrator exam strategy: (a) first pass — read every lesson in order without skipping, taking notes on concepts that feel unfamiliar; (b) second pass — work every scenario and lab, reading the 'why' explanations even for correct answers; (c) final pass — take the timed mock under realistic conditions (no pauses, no references).

How to read the scenarios: every scenario has a 'why' explanation — read it even when you got the answer right, because it explains the WRONG answers too (and real exams design wrong answers from those same misconceptions). The hint is there to unblock you, not to give away the answer.

Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key concepts out loud in your own words. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet — re-read that section.
Spaced repetition: revisit completed domains after 2-3 days. The bootcamp tracks your progress — use the dashboard to identify weak areas and drill those specifically before the mock.

example.code:
Week 1: Start Here + first 3 domains (lessons only)
Week 2: Remaining domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3: All labs + weak-area review
Week 4: Timed mock → review misses → targeted re-study
Exam/Interview: Confident and prepared
example.walkthrough: This 4-week plan assumes 1-2 hours per day. Adjust the pace to your schedule, but keep the order: lessons before scenarios, scenarios before labs, everything before the mock. The mock is a diagnostic tool — take it when you're ready to find gaps, not when you're still learning fundamentals.

pitfalls: Skipping the Start Here domain because 'I already know the basics' — the study strategy and terminology sections prevent wasted effort later.
Doing scenarios before reading the lessons — you'll memorize answers without understanding the concepts, and the mock will expose it.
Ignoring the 'why' explanations for correct answers — the wrong-answer analysis is where deep understanding comes from.
Taking the mock too early as a 'practice test' — it's a final validation, not a study tool. Use it once when ready.

lessons.title: Red Hat Certified System Administrator: Field Overview and Key Terminology
concepts: Red Hat Certified System Administrator sits at the intersection of theory and hands-on practice. The professionals who excel are those who can both explain the 'why' and execute the 'how' under pressure.

Key terminology is the price of admission — every domain in this bootcamp assumes you can use the core vocabulary precisely. When you encounter an unfamiliar term, stop and learn it before continuing.
The field rewards systems thinkers: people who see how components connect, not just isolated facts. The Systems Anatomy domain teaches this explicitly — start there after finishing Start Here.
Documentation is a professional skill, not an afterthought. As you learn, practice explaining concepts as if writing a runbook — clear, sequential, with the 'why' for each step.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'I know about X.'
Strong answer: 'X works by [mechanism]. In practice, I've used it to [application]. The key consideration is [tradeoff].'
example.walkthrough: This is the answer framework for interviews and exams: mechanism → application → tradeoff. Every lesson in this bootcamp is structured to build this three-part understanding. Practice using it from day one.

pitfalls: Using jargon without understanding — interviewers will probe deeper, and vague terminology collapses under follow-up questions.
Learning tools before concepts — tools change, but the underlying principles persist across versions and vendors.
Neglecting the 'boring' fundamentals — advanced topics assume solid foundations, and gaps there compound.
lessons.try_it: Write a one-paragraph explanation of what a professional in this field does daily. Be specific — name the systems, the tasks, and the decisions.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: From Learning to Mastery
concepts: The learning pyramid: reading alone retains ~10%, but teaching someone else retains ~90%. After each domain, explain the concepts to an imaginary colleague — or better, a real one.
Deliberate practice: don't just re-read weak areas, actively test yourself on them. The scenario drills are designed for this — they force retrieval, not recognition.
Error analysis: every wrong answer is data. Log your misses by domain and concept. Patterns in your errors reveal exactly where to focus.
The 80/20 rule: 80% of exam/interview questions come from 20% of the material — the core concepts that everything else builds on. This bootcamp front-loads those in the early domains.
Sleep consolidates learning: study sessions followed by sleep outperform cramming. Don't sacrifice rest for extra hours — your brain needs downtime to build connections.

example.code:
Study session template (60 min):
  0-10:  Review previous session's key concepts (retrieval)
  10-40: New lesson + scenario practice (learning)
  40-50: Lab exercise (application)
  50-60: Write summary notes (consolidation)

End each session by writing tomorrow's starting point.
example.walkthrough: This template prevents the two biggest study failures: passive re-reading (no retrieval) and marathon sessions (diminishing returns). The 10-minute review at the start compounds over weeks — by exam day, early material is rock solid.

pitfalls: Cramming the night before — it produces familiarity (recognition) without recall ability, which is what exams test.
Studying only strengths because it feels good — the discomfort of weak areas is where growth happens.
No error log — without tracking misses, you repeat the same mistakes and can't measure improvement.
Isolation — discussing concepts with others (or writing about them) exposes gaps that solo study hides.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log now — a simple document with columns for date, domain, concept missed, and correct understanding. You'll use this throughout.

lessons.title: What Success Looks Like: Exam and Interview Readiness
concepts: Readiness isn't a feeling — it's measurable. You're ready when: (a) mock scores are consistently above the passing threshold, (b) you can explain any lesson's key concepts without notes, (c) scenario misses are rare and random (not clustered in one domain).
For exams: time management is a skill to practice. The mock simulates real timing — use it to calibrate your pace (e.g., if the exam allows 2 minutes per question, practice at that pace).
For interviews: prepare stories, not just answers. 'Tell me about a time when...' needs specific examples. As you work labs, note what you built and what went wrong — these become interview stories.
The night before: no new material. Review your error log, skim key concept summaries, and rest. Confidence comes from preparation, not last-minute cramming.
A Linux system administrator is expected to handle ambiguity. Exams and interviews test this with incomplete scenarios — practice making reasonable assumptions and stating them explicitly.

example.code:
Readiness checklist:
  [ ] All lessons completed with passing knowledge checks
  [ ] All scenarios attempted, error log reviewed
  [ ] All labs completed successfully
  [ ] Mock score above target (with time to spare)
  [ ] Can whiteboard core concepts from memory
  [ ] Error patterns addressed (no clustered weaknesses)
example.walkthrough: Go through this checklist honestly one week before your target date. Any unchecked item is a priority. If multiple items are unchecked, consider adjusting your timeline — rushing into an exam unprepared wastes time and money.

pitfalls: Confusing completion with mastery — finishing all lessons doesn't mean you're ready; the mock score is the real indicator.
Ignoring time pressure in practice — untimed perfection doesn't transfer to timed exams.
No interview stories prepared — technical knowledge without communication skills underperforms in interviews.

lessons.title: Capstone Project: Build Your Red Hat Certified System Administrator Portfolio Piece
concepts: A portfolio project proves you can DO the work, not just answer questions about it. Employers and interviewers remember what you built far longer than what you scored.
Choose a project that demonstrates the full lifecycle: planning → implementation → testing → documentation → presentation. A Linux system administrator is expected to own work end-to-end.
Scope ruthlessly: a small project done well beats an ambitious project done poorly. Pick something you can complete in 2-4 weekends.
Document as you build, not after. Future-you (and interviewers) need to understand your decisions, not just your results.
Make it visible: GitHub repository with a professional README, architecture diagram, and demo instructions. If it's not on GitHub, it didn't happen.

example.code:
Project structure:
  README.md          # What, why, how to run
  docs/
    architecture.md  # System design and decisions
    setup.md         # Step-by-step build guide
  src/               # Your implementation
  tests/             # Validation that it works
  demo/              # Screenshots or video walkthrough
example.walkthrough: This structure signals professionalism. The README is your first impression — write it for someone who's never seen the project. The architecture doc shows you think before you build. Tests prove it works. Start with the README (write what you'll build), then implement.

pitfalls: Tutorial hell — following a guide step-by-step without understanding teaches nothing. Build something original, even if small.
No documentation — undocumented code is unusable code, and interviewers will ask you to explain your decisions.
Perfectionism paralysis — ship a working v1, then iterate. A deployed simple project beats an unreleased complex one.
Skipping the 'why' — every technical choice needs a reason. 'I used X because...' is an interview question waiting to happen.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Work: From Build to Interview Story
concepts: The STAR method for technical stories: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what you did, specifically) → Result (measurable outcome).
Lead with the problem, not the technology. 'We needed to automate X because manual process took Y hours' is more compelling than 'I used tool Z.'
Quantify everything: time saved, errors reduced, performance improved, users served. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
Prepare for deep dives: interviewers will pick one detail and probe. Know your architecture cold — every component, every tradeoff, every alternative you considered.
Show the messy parts: what went wrong, how you debugged it, what you'd do differently. This demonstrates maturity more than a flawless narrative.

example.code:
Weak: 'I built a thing with React.'
Strong: 'Our team spent 6 hours weekly on manual deployments. I built an automated pipeline using [tools] that cut deployment time to 15 minutes and eliminated config drift. The hardest part was [challenge] — I solved it by [approach].'
example.walkthrough: Notice the structure: problem (6 hours wasted) → action (built pipeline) → result (15 min, no drift) → depth (hardest part + solution). Practice telling your capstone story in 2 minutes, then be ready to go deep on any part.

pitfalls: Vague claims without specifics — 'I improved performance' means nothing; 'I reduced load time from 4s to 800ms by...' is compelling.
Only preparing the happy path — interviewers specifically ask about failures and challenges.
Memorizing a script — stories should feel conversational, not rehearsed. Know the beats, not the words.
No demo ready — always have a live demo, screenshots, or video. 'Let me show you' beats 'trust me.'

lessons.title: Beyond the Capstone: Continuous Growth
concepts: The capstone is a starting point, not a finish line. The best Linux system administrators are continuous learners — the field evolves, and so should you.
Build in public: share your learnings (blog posts, conference talks, open source contributions). Teaching solidifies your knowledge and builds your professional reputation.
Find your niche: general competence gets you hired, but deep expertise in a specific area makes you indispensable. Use the capstone to explore what energizes you.
Mentor others: explaining concepts to junior colleagues is the fastest way to deepen your own understanding and develop leadership skills.
Stay current: follow key practitioners, read release notes, experiment with new tools in a lab. Allocate 2-3 hours weekly to deliberate learning.

example.code:
Growth plan template:
  Monthly: One deep-dive (new tool, advanced concept)
  Quarterly: One shareable output (blog, talk, contribution)
  Annually: One significant skill addition (certification, major project)

  Track: What did I learn? What did I build? What did I teach?
example.walkthrough: This isn't about hustle culture — it's about intentional growth. The monthly deep-dive keeps you sharp, the quarterly output builds your portfolio, the annual skill prevents stagnation. Adjust the pace to your life, but keep the habit.

pitfalls: Stopping after the capstone — skills atrophy without use. Keep building, even small things.
Learning without applying — knowledge without practice fades quickly. Always pair learning with doing.
No community — solo learning is slower and lonelier. Find peers, join groups, contribute.

lessons.title: Partitioning Tools
concepts: parted for GPT (modern, >2TB disks); fdisk for MBR (legacy, <2TB)
GPT is the default — supports 128 partitions, no extended/logical complexity
Always verify with lsblk and blkid after partitioning — don't trust memory
partprobe or reboot to re-read the partition table after changes

example.code:
# Create GPT partition
parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary xfs 1MiB 10GiB
# Format and mount
mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
mkdir /data
mount /dev/sdb1 /data
# Persistent: add to /etc/fstab
UUID=$(blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sdb1)
echo "UUID=$UUID /data xfs defaults 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
example.walkthrough: Use UUID in fstab, not /dev/sdb1 — device names change; UUIDs don't. Test with mount -a before rebooting.

pitfalls: Device names in fstab — /dev/sdb1 today might be /dev/sdc1 after reboot
Forgetting mount -a test — a typo in fstab means boot failure
No backup of partition table — sgdisk --backup saves you from disasters
lessons.try_it: Create a partition, format it, add to fstab by UUID, and verify with mount -a and a reboot.

lessons.title: LVM Deep Dive
concepts: LVM layers: Physical Volumes (disks) → Volume Groups (pools) → Logical Volumes (usable partitions)
Advantage over raw partitions: resize online, span multiple disks, snapshots
Extend: lvextend -r (the -r resizes filesystem too — don't forget it!)
Reduce: trickier — unmount, fsck, resize fs, then lvreduce (order matters!)

example.code:
# Create LVM
pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
lvcreate -n lvapp -L 20G vgdata
mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvapp
# Extend online
lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vgdata/lvapp
example.walkthrough: The -r flag is critical — without it, the LV grows but the filesystem doesn't. You'll have unusable space.

pitfalls: Forgetting -r on extend — LV bigger but filesystem unchanged
Reducing mounted filesystems — unmount first (except XFS, which can't shrink at all)
No VG free space monitoring — extensions fail when VG is full
lessons.try_it: Create an LVM setup, extend it online, take a snapshot, then practice reducing (on ext4, not XFS).

lessons.title: ACLs Beyond ugo
concepts: Standard permissions (ugo/rwx) are insufficient for complex sharing — ACLs provide fine-grained control
setfacl -m u:alice:rw file — grant Alice read/write without changing owner/group
getfacl to view — the '+' in ls -l indicates ACLs are present
Default ACLs on directories propagate to new files — essential for shared directories

example.code:
# Shared project directory
mkdir /projects/app1
setfacl -m g:developers:rwx /projects/app1
setfacl -d -m g:developers:rwx /projects/app1
setfacl -m u:alice:rwx /projects/app1
# Verify
getfacl /projects/app1

# Need a boolean?

setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
# Analyze denials
sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log

labs.objective: Enable only required services at boot and expose exactly one application port through firewalld.
steps: List enabled services with 'systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled' and identify anything unnecessary.
Disable and stop one unneeded service with 'systemctl disable --now <service>'.
Enable the application service persistently: 'systemctl enable --now myapp'.
Add its port permanently: 'firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8443/tcp' then 'firewall-cmd --reload'.
Verify with 'systemctl is-enabled myapp' and 'firewall-cmd --list-ports'.

labs.title: Relocate a web root under SELinux
labs.objective: Move a document root to a nonstandard path and make it serve correctly with SELinux enforcing.
steps: Create /srv/www, place an index.html, and confirm 403s with SELinux enforcing.
Read the denial with 'ausearch -m avc -ts recent' and note the wrong file type with 'ls -Z'.
Declare the correct type: 'semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/www(/.*)?"'.
Apply it: 'restorecon -Rv /srv/www' and verify with 'ls -Z'.
Confirm the page serves and that 'getenforce' still reports Enforcing.

labs.title: LVM lifecycle: extend and snapshot
labs.objective: Extend a logical volume online and practice snapshot-based rollback.
steps: Inspect the stack: 'pvs', 'vgs', 'lvs', and 'lsblk -f' to map PV→VG→LV→filesystem.
Extend an LV: 'lvextend -r -L +2G <lv-path>' and verify with 'df -h'.
Create a snapshot: 'lvcreate -s -n snap_test -L 1G <lv-path>'.
Write a canary file, then 'lvconvert --merge' the snapshot (after unmount if required) to roll back.
Verify the canary file is gone and remove leftover snapshots.

checks.hint: List logical volumes to see the snapshot.

labs.objective: Practice GRUB-level recovery by booting to rescue target and fixing a bad fstab.
steps: In a test VM, add a bogus entry to /etc/fstab (nonexistent UUID) and reboot.
At the GRUB menu, press 'e', add 'systemd.unit=rescue.target' to the linux line, boot with Ctrl-X.
In the rescue shell, run 'blkid' and correct the fstab entry.
Run 'systemctl daemon-reload' then 'systemctl default' to continue booting.
Confirm clean boot and remove the practice entry.

checks.hint: Check the current target while in rescue mode.

simulations.brief: A user cannot log in. /etc/passwd shows their shell as /bin/false and their account is not locked — but SSH rejects them.
simulations.debrief: /bin/false as a login shell means the account can never get an interactive shell — common for service accounts, wrong for humans. The fix is chsh/usermod to set a real shell. Always read the passwd entry before resetting passwords.

evidence: sshd: User ops not allowed because shell /bin/false does not exist or is not executable... wait, it exists
steps.explain: The shell field is /bin/false — the account is configured to never allow interactive login. This is correct for service accounts but wrong for a human operator. Fix with usermod -s /bin/bash ops.

sections.heading: Storage (LVM/Stratis)
items: LVM layers bottom-up — PV (physical volume on the disk/partition) → VG (pool) → LV (carved from the pool) → filesystem → mount. pvcreate labels the device, vgcreate pools it, lvcreate carves the LV, mkfs creates the filesystem, then mount/fstab.
UUIDs and LABELs are written on the filesystem and never change — 'UUID=xxx /data xfs defaults 0 2' survives rescans.
Lvextend — Lvextend grows the block device; '-r/--resizefs' then grows the filesystem appropriately (xfs_growfs for XFS, resize2fs for ext4) — online, no unmount.
XFS — XFS can only grow, never shrink; ext4 can do both (shrinking requires unmount + e2fsck). XFS is grow-only by design — there is no shrink support (xfs_growfs only grows).
